articles.title: UK economy grows at fastest rate for more than two years
articles.text:
The UK economy grew at its fastest rate for more than two years in the three months to September.

Between July and September, the economy expanded by 0.7%, accelerating from the previous three months, official figures, external show.

The robust growth suggests a far more resilient economy than expected over the summer, despite the impact of higher energy prices from the Iran war.

Strong growth in the services sector - the largest part of the economy, which includes non-physical goods such as consultancy services and computer programming as well as hotels and restaurants - helped boost the numbers.

Within services, computer programming registered its fastest growth for the past three years, helped by cloud computing and AI-linked spending.

The boost from computer programming and consultancy services has been the biggest driver of growth so far this year.

Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the Office for National Statistics, said it was "possible growth could have been even stronger" if there hadn't been a war in the Middle East.

But he says households may still not feel better off, and that prices might soon start to rise more quickly than wages.

However, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the figures were "welcome news".

"Despite a year where events around the world have pushed up costs here at home, our economy is growing, bringing hope for the future," he said.

Chancellor John Healey told the BBC the figures showed a "remarkable resilience" in the face of global conflicts, and hopes they "bring back confidence in Britain".

Asked about how government decisions could be the reason for growth when AI investment has been a main driver, Healey said ministers can always "help or hinder" business confidence and investments.

articles.title: 5 Big Questions as C.E.O.s Meet in China
articles.text:
U.S.-Chinese business relations were thrown a curveball ahead of a major C.E.O. summit in Shenzhen, China, next week. On Thursday, Jensen Huang resigned as the chief executive of Nvidia after it was revealed that he had affairs with an executive at the company and a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

One of the architects of the artificial intelligence boom, Huang was also perhaps the strongest proponent in Washington for U.S. companies selling A.I. hardware to China — an issue that has become central to the countries’ fraught economic relationship. Huang, who has a close relationship to President Trump, has also promoted open A.I. models, an approach favored by many Chinese firms.

China hawks in Congress have already seized on the scandal, using it to push for three bills that would put more restrictions on technology exports to the country.

Next week’s summit, which is hosted by the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, has the potential to advance policy talks. Trump and the Chinese leader Xi Jinping (and perhaps President Vladimir Putin of Russia) are expected to meet. On the sidelines, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will take part in a bilateral dialogue on A.I.

But observers have low expectations for big changes. “The Chinese would like to prolong this fragile stability for as long as they can,” Ryan Hass, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution who advised President Barack Obama and White House officials on U.S. policy toward China, told DealBook.

Still, amid a stalled trade war, expanding export controls, legal tussles and suspected spy games, the conversation may have just gotten a little more complicated. Here are the biggest questions looming about the world’s most important economic relationship.

1. Does America clamp down further on the export of advanced chips?

The U.S. has banned its most advanced A.I chips, like Nvidia’s Blackwell, from reaching China — though, given reports of chip smuggling operations in Singapore, Taiwan and elsewhere, perhaps to limited effect.

In designing and manufacturing advanced semiconductors, China’s capabilities still lag those of the U.S. and Taiwan. Hawks want to keep it that way. But Trump has been less than resolute. In January, his administration allowed sales of Nvidia’s less powerful H200 to China, a move that is now being scrutinized by Congress in the wake of Huang’s resignation.

On Capitol Hill, a handful of proposed pieces of legislation could severely restrict China’s access. “Given how vocal Congress has been on this topic, and given the fact that Congress is going to be more empowered post-midterms, it’s less likely we get a loosening of chip rules and more likely we get a tightening,” said Chris Miller, author of “Chip War: The Fight for the World’s Most Critical Technology.”

On the other side of the chip coin are foreign data centers, which have largely escaped Washington’s attention. That may soon change, too. Lawmakers in Congress have been pushing for tighter limits on Chinese companies’ renting computing power abroad, whether from U.S.-owned data centers or facilities running American chips.

This month, the U.S. firm Oracle canceled a roughly $7 billion contract that gave Tencent, a Chinese company, access to advanced A.I. chips in data centers in Southeast Asia, after U.S. officials raised concerns, according to The Financial Times. In 2027, U.S. cloud giants like Microsoft and Amazon could face similar scrutiny for hosting open-weight models from Chinese labs such as Moonshot and Z.ai, said Paul Triolo, partner at DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group, a global advisory firm.

If the U.S. further restricts access to chips, China would probably retaliate by restricting access to rare earths and the powerful magnets made from them, which go into products as varied as electric vehicles and fighter jets. “We’re sort of on the brink here,” Triolo said. “If the Chinese escalate further on rare-earths export controls, we’re in uncharted territory.”

2. Does China further barricade its tech economy?

In Shenzhen, U.S. tech executives will probably press for more leniency for their companies in China. On the whole, observers said, they’re unlikely to get it. In May, Bloomberg reported that China had begun requiring senior A.I. researchers and executives at private firms like Alibaba and DeepSeek to get approval before traveling abroad, with some surrendering their passports. The authorities also barred the two Chinese founders of Manus, an A.I. start-up based in Singapore, from leaving China after the company was acquired by Meta, then ordered Meta to unwind the deal.

This month, Chinese regulators blocked SoftBank’s $5.4 billion acquisition of a robotics firm on national security grounds. And China’s own export control list — which includes not just rare earths but also batteries and industrial machinery related to solar panels and tunnel boring — is lengthening.

“In 2027, we should expect more of this,” said Rush Doshi, a political scientist at Georgetown University who oversaw China policy in the Biden administration. “Every two weeks, there’s new announcements from China. It’s all in the same direction.”

3. Can America make progress on rare earths?

China dominates the market for rare earths. In 2025, Beijing responded to U.S. tariffs and semiconductor controls with a series of sweeping export restrictions on these elements, which forced the Trump administration to back down.

U.S. policymakers have since scrambled to erode that dependence. So far, more than $2.5 billion in federal loans and equity has flowed into American rare earth companies like MP Materials, which operates the country’s only producing rare earth mine, and USA Rare Earth, which is building a mine-to-magnet supply chain in Texas and Oklahoma. Washington is also striking mining deals abroad, in Australia, Brazil, Saudi Arabia and elsewhere. Still, experts said such efforts would take years to bear fruit.

“Until new rare-earths processing facilities and permanent magnet manufacturing capabilities come online, it will continue to feature as a bargaining tool by the Chinese,” said Gracelin Baskaran, a director of the Critical Minerals Security Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

4. Does the trade war truce hold long term or disintegrate?

In April 2025, after “Liberation Day” set off a tit-for-tat escalation with Beijing, tariffs on Chinese goods reached as high as 145 percent. A month later, after bilateral talks in Geneva, those fell to 30 percent. In October 2025, on the sidelines of an APEC summit in Busan, South Korea, Trump and Xi struck a truce. Washington agreed to lower the rate further while Beijing paused its rare-earth export controls and agreed to buy American agricultural products and Boeing jets.

China, according to industry observers, has not followed through on its promises. This month, the White House voiced its displeasure with Beijing, a move officials might reiterate in Shenzhen. On Jan. 10, the Busan agreement is set to expire. Instead of extending it, the Trump administration may take new offensive measures, such as financial sanctions against Chinese companies.

“The current U.S.-China détente could come apart,” Doshi said.

In 2027, the trade war could resume in earnest. Would that mean decoupling continues? This year, American exports to China barely recovered from a 26 percent plunge in 2025, the steepest in recent history. Chinese exports to the U.S. were down about 11 percent through September, though they have been climbing since the spring, as China’s global trade surplus surpassed $1 trillion. Washington has also continued to restrict Chinese technology. Still, Bessent said this week that Washington’s intent is to “de-risk, not to decouple” with China.

In September, the countries announced a 30-for-30 deal: China would lower barriers on $30 billion of U.S. exports, and the U.S. would lower barriers on $30 billion of Chinese imports. The sides have exchanged product lists, but the deal still awaits domestic legal confirmation.

5. Does a black swan take flight?

Some years ago, Xi ordered his military forces to be ready for a successful invasion of Taiwan by 2027. The Chinese leader will be 74 next year and presumably contemplating his legacy. With a new term likely beginning and a Trump presidency waning, will he give the order? Or will a conflict finally erupt over contested territories in the South China Sea? A great power war is the blackest of black swans.

But there is also the potential for an A.I.-enabled cyberattack that wreaks havoc in either China or the U.S., Triolo said. Or the semiconductor market could implode in some way, Miller added. As Xi warned Communist Party cadres last month, “Be ready at all times to withstand the major tests of high winds, choppy waters and even stormy seas.”

IN CASE YOU MISSED IT

The Jensen Huang scandal rocked Wall Street, Washington and Silicon Valley. The future of Nvidia’s prolific investing, which has helped fuel the A.I. boom at a delicate time for the industry, was thrown into uncertainty. And President Trump is facing scrutiny over what he knew about the allegations against Huang.

Anthropic set a price range for its I.P.O. The range, of $70 to $78 a share, would make the company worth $1.26 trillion to $1.41 trillion. Nvidia’s partners have agreed to buy billions of dollars’ worth of stock at the final I.P.O. price. At the high end, the public offering, expected on Thursday, could raise as much as $100 billion. That would be a new record.

Home sales fell to a record low. Sales of existing homes fell last month to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million, the lowest level since 2010 and a sign of consumer weakness. Mortgage rates slid for the fourth consecutive week but remained above 7 percent.

More big deals: SpaceX plans to spend $74 billion on data centers in Texas and Arizona. Kalshi cut ties with Donald Trump Jr. And work in some offices ground to a halt after a global outage disrupted Microsoft services.

Can you future-proof your kids?

The first thing that Daniel Susskind wants you to know about his new book, “What Should My Children Do?,” is that his answers probably aren’t as specific as you would like them to be. “I think a really important starting point is to give up on the idea of future-proofing, that if only we think deeply and cleverly enough about the future, we’ll be able to predict exactly what jobs are going to have to be done, and then say exactly which advanced skills we ought to teach young people,” he said.

Susskind, an economist and a professor of business at Gresham College in London, talked with Sarah Kessler about what we can do. The conversation has been condensed and edited.

How should parents prepare their children for the future, if not with specific skills?

I think one of the most important things we can do is get back to basics: literacy, numeracy and critical thinking.

And I think we ought to be spending about a third of our time now in primary, secondary, university, professional, in work, teaching people to make effective use of these technologies.

The big challenge is how you can do both, how you can encourage young people to use these technologies without at the same time undermining these basics.

So how do you do both?

We were here in the 1980s with the arrival of the electronic calculator, which provoked exactly the same sorts of worries. Why bother learning to do a difficult calculation if this powerful little computer in your pocket could do it for you?

The approach was to say, we need to do both. We essentially took maths education in the U.K. and divided it in two, and said: “We’ve got to spend part of our time teaching young people to use this technology and solve problems that would have been unimaginable before. But we also need to spend parts of our time without it, making sure that arithmetic stays sharp.”

And crucially, we need to test both at the end. I call this “teach both, test both.” And that’s what I think we need to do now across education.

The calculator example kind of falls apart in the business world. There is a good deal of learning that happens on the job, and employers rely on that to build their employees into experts. But they’re not necessarily willing to make employees do work that a machine could do much faster. So what do you think is the best route there?

articles.title: This Man Stole $9 Million in Gold Bars on the Upper West Side, Police Say
articles.text:
The meeting point had been arranged: near 81st Street and Broadway on the Upper West Side.

It was there, in broad daylight, that two men approached each other on a Wednesday in April 2025. One of the men, a 67-year-old New Yorker, transported a bag of $9 million in gold bars, each one the size of a chocolate bar, that the police said someone online had instructed him to buy and hand over.

The man did exactly as he was told, believing that he could secure his financial assets, which an alert on his computer had led him to believe were compromised, the authorities said.

The other man took the sack of gold and fled on foot, according to the police. The first man had been the victim of an online fraud.

Now, more than a year and a half after the deceit, the New York Police Department is asking for the public’s help in identifying the man who ran off with the gold bars in connection with a grand larceny investigation.

Investigators this week released security camera footage and images of the man suspected of taking the bars.

Isaac Kahan, the owner of Bullion Trading LLC, a gold and silver dealer in Manhattan’s Diamond District, wondered about the sheer logistics that were involved in the heist.

Each of the gold bars weighs one kilogram, about 2.2 pounds, according to the police. While the dollar value of gold has fluctuated since 2025, the current cost of a one-kilo bar is about $130,000, according to Mr. Kahan, meaning that $9 million would buy about 69 gold bars and weigh more than 150 pounds.

“I don’t even know how he would be able to carry that,” Mr. Kahan said in an interview on Friday. “You can’t even lift that.”

From his decades as a precious metals wholesaler, Mr. Kahan said, he had become all too familiar with such fraud schemes, which he noted typically target people in their 70s and 80s, and seek to get them to liquidate their assets to buy gold.

About once every two weeks, Mr. Kahan’s business will receive somewhat cryptic requests from potential clients to buy gold bars, he said, adding that it used to happen on a daily basis. Unlike investors, victims of frauds show little interest in the weight and purity of gold, he said.

“When a person starts throwing the dollar amount first to me, that’s a telltale sign right away,” Mr. Kahan said.

A few years ago, while his company was closed for the Jewish High Holy Days of Rosh Hashana and Yom Kippur, it received several online orders from people who had been targets of such schemes, he said. The business was able to cancel some of the transactions, according to Mr. Kahan, who said one victim’s daughter had contacted him after noticing a suspicious wire transfer for $150,000.

“It was heartbreaking,” Mr. Kahan said, adding that gold is essentially “impossible” to trace.

An older woman in Florida was the target of a similar scheme this May, according to the F.B.I., which said the victim received an email claiming to be from Amazon and telling her to call a phone number because her bank account had been breached.

A person claiming to be associated with the bank told the woman that her identity had been stolen and that her Social Security number had been compromised, which would require her to speak with another individual, who claimed to be an agent with the Federal Trade Commission.

That individual instructed the woman to write a check for $101,220 to buy 21 gold bars that she delivered to a masked man in a Volvo at a Sunoco gas station near the victim’s home in McIntosh, Fla., the authorities said.

When the woman received directions to buy another $500,000 in gold bars, a friend became suspicious, according to federal authorities, who began an investigation and this month announced the indictments of 10 people in connection with the fraud scheme.

It was not clear if there was any connection between the cases in Florida and New York.

The F.B.I. field office in New York did not respond to a request for comment on Friday about the gold bars that were stolen from the man on the Upper West Side.

Mr. Kahan said that he flags suspicious gold purchases for the F.B.I. and arranges for agents to speak to people who he fears could be the targets of frauds.

“We do try to slow the process down,” he said.

articles.title: He Was China’s Man in Panama. Then He Became a Wanted Man.
articles.text:
For years, Zhang Liang warned that powerful people in his former homeland, China, would try to drag him back. Then one Saturday morning in July, it happened.

In Panama City, two police officers on motorbikes pulled alongside his black Mercedes-Benz and motioned him to stop. A check of his identification turned up an Interpol red notice from the Chinese authorities, who wanted him extradited on charges of embezzling around $300 million.

Mr. Zhang, a 44-year-old dealmaker, barely had time to remove his gray suit jacket and wrap it around his head before officers handcuffed him and paraded him before cameras at Interpol’s National Central Bureau in Panama.

He has been behind bars ever since.

It was a remarkable fall for Mr. Zhang, one that traces the arc of China’s dealings with the West. He went to Panama ready to make deals and help China extend its influence. He oversaw a port project that promised to turn a former U.S. military base near the Panama Canal’s Atlantic entrance into Latin America’s largest container terminal, establishing a base for Chinese interests near one of the world’s busiest trade routes.

To his aggrieved former business partners, though, Mr. Zhang is a corporate fugitive who used offshore jurisdictions and other people’s money to enrich himself. He wooed Panama’s elite with promises of deals and funding that never materialized. He continued to earn a salary of $6,300 a month, his lawyers said at a bail hearing, a substantial sum in Panama.

His tailored suits, A. Lange & Söhne wristwatch and black Mercedes all pointed to a lavish lifestyle. Mr. Zhang has faced lawsuits, criminal complaints and judicial proceedings in multiple jurisdictions. He is also pursuing an international arbitration claim against Panama.

The competing accounts of victim and culprit are difficult to reconcile. The ownership of the port is disputed, and the financial dealings behind it are opaque. After reviewing the case, Panama’s Foreign Affairs Ministry agreed last month to proceed with Mr. Zhang’s extradition to China, according to a document seen by The Times.

The Foreign Affairs Ministries of China and Panama did not respond to emailed questions.

For a decade, Mr. Zhang had used China’s growing interest in Panama to expand his influence. Now, as Beijing and Washington battle over the canal, his business empire has unraveled, and the political connections that once helped him prosper offer little protection.

This account, with previously unreported details, is based on official documents, legal filings and interviews with lawyers and associates, including a former colleague who has accused local authorities in China of harassment, coercion and the falsifying of records in Mr. Zhang’s case.

Mr. Zhang arrived in Panama in 2016 to oversee investments for a wealthy Chinese financier. A lawyer licensed in New York and China, he had been named a “leading talent” by China’s Justice Ministry.

From an 18th-floor office overlooking Panama Bay, Mr. Zhang secured Panama’s approval to build, own and operate a major container terminal in a free-trade zone on Margarita Island.

Chinese state-controlled media celebrated the deal as a diplomatic coup, advancing investment interests in Panama. Mr. Zhang also secured a deal to build a gas-fired power plant. He promised officials that the project would create 1,000 jobs and lower energy costs.

“Margarita Island gave them a lot of access and intelligence value,” said Isaac B. Kardon, an adjunct professor at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies who specializes in Chinese maritime strategy.

But the political opening started to close.

Mr. Varela left office in 2019, and his successor was far less receptive to Chinese investment. The Panamanian government began moving against the Margarita Island project.

Mr. Zhang sought Beijing’s help. Tingyun Han, his former assistant and translator, said she had gone to the Chinese Embassy in Panama City, hoping officials could persuade the Panamanian government to reconsider. The plea went nowhere.

The new Panamanian government “no longer wanted any Asian faces or Chinese enterprises involved,” Ms. Han told The Times from China.

Mr. Zhang’s problems deepened when his backer, a wealthy property financier named Gao Tianguo, lost his fortune. Mr. Gao’s lending businesses in China collapsed under billions of dollars of debt. He was arrested in 2020 and died two years later.

In 2022, Mr. Zhang agreed to transfer the port assets to Notarc Management Group, a Bahamas and Florida-based private equity firm. Within months, the deal incited an ownership dispute. Ye Cheng, a politically connected Chinese businessman who claimed a controlling stake in the project, accused Mr. Zhang of illegally seizing the company.

But Panamanian authorities declined to bring charges, concluding that Mr. Ye’s allegations amounted to a commercial dispute. Mr. Ye’s company, the Landbridge Group, did not reply to requests for comment.

China took a different view.

In 2023, police officers pulled Ms. Han, Mr. Zhang’s former assistant, off a plane in her home city of Xian and drove her 12 hours to Rizhao, where Mr. Ye’s company has its headquarters, she said. Officers interrogated her so intensely about Mr. Zhang and the port deal, she said, that she vomited and was taken to a hospital. She later accused the local police of torture.

Mr. Zhang became convinced that his adversaries in China were coming after him. In court filings in 2024, he described being followed to work by a white Nissan and chased through Panama City. He requested and received police protection.

China vowed to “take all necessary measures” to defend its interests in Panama. Chinese authorities started detaining hundreds of Panamanian-flagged vessels in China for inspection, disrupting trade.

Mr. Zhang was arrested the same week that China’s new ambassador arrived in Panama — and just five days before Panamanian officials were due in Beijing for talks to defuse the diplomatic standoff.

Panama’s foreign minister later said China had renewed a key maritime agreement that grants Panamanian-flagged ships preferential access to its ports.

“From the moment they arrested him — and that is no coincidence — the disputes between China and Panama disappeared,” said Guillermo Cochez, a Panamanian diplomat and one of Mr. Zhang’s lawyers.

No evidence links his arrest to the diplomatic negotiations. But relations between China and Panama improved afterward. Extradition documents revealed that Beijing wanted control of Mr. Zhang’s assets in Panama without explicitly asking for the port project.

articles.title: A ‘Generational Clash’ Is Fueling Europe’s Protests
articles.text:
Sébastien Ducros, a French data analyst who supports the widespread student protests in his country, has identified an obvious culprit for the lack of government funds for dilapidated schools.

“A huge portion of the money is going toward retirees, while many other things are being neglected,” said Mr. Ducros, 36. “I honestly think — even if it feels strange to say — that people like my parents are in a position where they should and could” surrender some of their pension payments, he added, saying that they were about to retire.

But Laurent Grinwald, 72, who retired recently after decades as a postal worker, isn’t eager for his pension to be reduced, particularly to pay for other state-funded services. Especially, he said, as rents and the cost of living have shot up.

“We’ve been working all this time,” Mr. Grinwald said, “and now, suddenly, the stance is, ‘Well, no, we’re going to start taking a bit more?’”

This disagreement embodies a broader question for Europe, one at the heart of the mass antigovernment demonstrations that returned to France on Saturday, as well as recent protests driven by frustrated young people in countries including Belgium, Germany, Greece, Italy and Portugal. As Europeans live longer, should the needs of the young be eclipsed by their parents’ and grandparents’ pensions, routinely the largest items in Europe’s national budgets?

“It’s a generational clash,” said Jorge Galindo, the director of EsadeEcPol, an independent think tank in Spain, which has some of the most generous pensions in Europe.

All of that, coupled with rising rents and house prices, has compounded a sense of generational injustice among young people. Only 38 percent of people aged 15 to 30 think that policymakers consider the long-term consequences of their decisions, according to a recent European Union survey. Only a third believe that today’s young people have the same shot at success as young people 30 years ago did, the survey also found.

The enormous financial burden of pensions — they gobble up around 40 percent of the spending on social protections in the European Union — has not been lost on European governments.

Over the past decade, many countries have tried to tinker with pension formulas, trying to cut costs while postponing major political blowback. To many older Europeans, pensions are considered the sacrosanct base of the European welfare system.

Often, they have avoided cutting what each retiree is paid while gradually raising the age at which citizens qualify for those payments — to 67 from 65, for example, or older. Denmark plans to raise it to 70 by 2040.

With one of the highest debt levels in Europe, France says it cannot afford to spend more on education — which has prompted the youth anger spurring the wave of unrest there.

On Saturday, protest marches took place across France for a fifth consecutive weekend. They were largely peaceful, despite clashes between black-clad agitators and the police in cities including Paris and Lyon. The Interior Ministry said the rallies drew 106,000 protesters, less than in recent weeks.

Other countries in Europe have tried other ways of softening the generational competition driving the continent’s protests. Britain plans to save billions by slowing the speed at which its pension payments increase over time, while Spain has enlarged its pool of taxpaying workers.

Spain chose in 2011 to raise its pension age to 67 in most cases. Then the current left-wing government enlarged the pension bill by ensuring that pension payments would grow in line with inflation, protecting recipients from rising prices but putting an enormous strain on the budget.

To offset those costs, it has bucked the European trend and opened its doors to immigrant labor — more than 1.7 million foreigners have entered the Spanish work force since 2018.

Those workers have increased tax revenue, which in turn helps to fund pension contributions, but eventually, experts note, they will age, too.

Spain will spend 17.3 percent of its gross domestic product in 2050 on pensions, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development — roughly four percentage points higher than now. That means the government would then be spending the equivalent in today’s terms of an additional $67 billion every year on pensions. It currently spends roughly $79 billion on education.

Despite the competition for resources, many of the young people protesting throughout Europe are loath to blame their elders.

“Honestly,” said Alice Cossa, 22, an Italian student who protested recently in Venice, “we’ve never talked about it.”

Left-wing demonstrators often say that pensions and other benefits can be funded by taxing the rich and corporations. Their right-wing counterparts suggest cutting immigration, blaming immigrants for soaking up welfare benefits.

Some feel, though, that at least some pensions, namely those received by wealthy older people, should be reassessed.

“We young people have less and less and less,” said Alejandro Rojano, 28, a bank employee who lives in a basement apartment in Madrid with a roommate. He said even his own nonagenarian grandparents received “way” more than his monthly salary, which was less than 2,000 euros, or less than $2,200. No political party would dare cut the benefits of such a dependable and powerful voting bloc as retirees, he lamented, adding of the pension payouts, “It makes no sense, you know?”

Mr. Galindo, the think tank director, said that given the entrenched political interests in protecting retirees, young people might need to form an essentially single-issue voting bloc. Because European governments are typically formed from coalitions of smaller parties, such a party could become pivotal and have its concerns taken seriously with only a handful of seats.

But young people are a shrinking demographic in Europe, and the number of older people, who are more likely to exercise political power through union and party memberships, is booming.

And young and middle-aged Europeans are reluctant to cut a benefit that they hope to enjoy in the future.

As Daniel Ramo, 46, left a recent teachers’ strike in Madrid protesting dismal salaries and packed classrooms, he said that he personally looked forward to receiving his generous Spanish pension after making €2,100 a month after taxes. In the meantime, the benefits of his parents’ pensions would trickle down to help him through tough times.

“I’m on strike knowing I’ll have to borrow money from my father,” said Mr. Ramo, who said his father’s pension made him the top earner in the family.

From the perspective of retirees, the hard-earned benefit helps keep families, and European society, going.

articles.title: Trump Administration Delays Enforcement of Medicaid Work Requirement
articles.text:
The Trump administration will allow states to delay enforcement of new rules requiring low-income adults to work in order to receive Medicaid coverage, according to a letter it sent on Friday to state Medicaid directors.

The announcement, which followed a recent loss in court over a key element of the work requirement, represents a major setback for a long-sought Republican reform. It comes less than two months before the work requirements were set to begin, on Jan. 1. States can now wait until July before ending coverage for people who do not meet the work requirement, the letter said.

In the letter, Dan Brillman, who oversees Medicaid at the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, acknowledged the significant burden states faced in building out new, expensive software systems to track the employment of enrollees. Hospitals have prepared massive education campaigns to help patients navigate the additional paperwork.

“We have heard directly from states about their implementation timelines, impediments to successful launches at scale,” Mr. Brillman wrote in the letter.

He added that the federal government still expected states in January to begin checking whether Medicaid enrollees are working. But for six months, they will not be required to cancel coverage for people who fail to comply, Mr. Brillman said.

The work requirement was enacted in the summer of 2025 as part of Republicans’ major tax and domestic policy legislation. It requires Medicaid enrollees without disabilities or young children to prove they worked, volunteered or attended school at least 80 hours a month in order to qualify for the program or continue enrollment in it.

The new requirement was expected to lead to substantial reductions in Medicaid coverage, disqualifying not only beneficiaries without jobs but also many who worked but were tripped up by documentation challenges. The Congressional Budget Office estimated that the policy would result in five million more Americans becoming uninsured over the next few years.

Democratic lawmakers fought the policy last year. Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the minority leader who is poised to become speaker when Democrats take over control of the House in January, has announced plans to vote on reversing the work requirement and other Medicaid cuts within the first 100 hours of the next Congress.

In court, 25 states and the District of Columbia had already won a six-month reprieve from some aspects of enforcing the work requirement. A federal judge in Massachusetts found that the Trump administration’s rules for defining who is too “medically frail” to comply with work requirements were stricter than the law allowed.

The January start date is specified in the text of the 2025 tax law. At a conference with state Medicaid officials last summer, where many expressed concerns about the timetable, Trump administration officials warned that no extensions would be coming.

“We know it’s going to be really hard for you to meet the deadline,” said Sara Vitolo, the deputy director for Medicaid. “It’s going to be hard for us. The expectation is going to be that we hit it. And that’s coming from the White House.”

The law also allows states to begin enforcing a work requirement early, and Nebraska and Montana have already begun their programs. In Nebraska, state officials estimate that more than 1,700 people have already been denied or lost Medicaid coverage due to the policy.

Christopher Rowland contributed reporting.

articles.title: Wall Street Makes Its Pitch for Anthropic’s I.P.O.
articles.text:
On Friday afternoon, on the 56th floor of JPMorgan’s headquarters, Jamie Dimon interviewed perhaps the most important man to Wall Street right now: Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic.

With less than one week before Anthropic plans to sell its shares on the open market, both men projected calm and confidence heading into what could be the largest initial public offering ever.

“We’re not super fussed on when exactly, what month, or what day, or what market conditions we go public into,” Dr. Amodei said, speaking on a small stage as thick clouds enveloped the New York skyline behind him.

Dr. Amodei’s nonchalance, though, belies the intensity of Wall Street’s efforts to sell Anthropic to investors. The company has lined up 22 banks, led by Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, to run its “roadshow,” a series of meetings and presentations, where investors hear about the company’s financials.

Anthropic disclosed earlier this week it aimed to raise up to $100 billion at a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion, down from $2 trillion bankers had floated this summer, before market jitters appeared.

JPMorgan and Citi are stewarding efforts to sell to individual investors, which Anthropic has said it expects to make up about 20 percent of the offering. Another critical group of investors: Seven of the tech industry’s biggest players, including Broadcom, Nvidia and Microsoft, which have already signed up to invest a total of $26 billion in Anthropic immediately after listing.

Each of those seven technology firms also stands to benefit from a successful Anthropic listing: Some, like Nvidia, Google and Microsoft, were already investors. All of them count Anthropic as a customer, and a successful Anthropic offering means a sustainable buyer of their services.

And the banks themselves could stand to collect roughly $400 million in fees on the deal, according to analysts at Evercore.

Anthropic is entering a market that has been less than ideal. Concerns about debt-fueled spending on artificial intelligence have whipsawed stock and bond prices for weeks. This week’s shocking resignation of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s chief executive added more turmoil and uncertainty.

“Everyone has an interest in making this a success,” said Craig Coben, a former global head of equity capital markets at Bank of America, describing Anthropic’s offering as “too crucial to fail.”

“So far the market thinks the A.I. ecosystem can withstand Huang’s resignation,” Mr. Coben said, “but it’s still processing in real time what it all means for future spend and investment.”

Throughout its roadshow, Anthropic’s messaging has been that it will try to control its own destiny. In private meetings in New York conference rooms and on video calls, executives have stressed to investors that the company will rise above the fray by using a new cash pile from the I.P.O. to develop its own chips and build their own data centers.

They’re also selling what is, for now, a dream. Dr. Amodei has spent significant time in meetings on a subject without much traction yet: the company’s early forays into helping to develop new drugs and automate science laboratories, two investors said.

Anthropic, and its advisers, have taken a notably more austere approach than Elon Musk’s SpaceX public offering in June, a reflection in part of Dr. Amodei’s more understated style.

Mr. Musk’s roadshow video that opened with orchestral music, a snapshot of the moon, and reference to Mr. Musk’s goal to “change mankind and make us a multi-planetary species.”

In Anthropic’s promotional video, Dr. Amodei, sporting a teal sweater that went with the earthy colors of his office backdrop, warns within the first few minutes of the potential of artificial intelligence to “make a bioweapon or do a cyberattack.” (Dr. Amodei did call artificial intelligence “the most promising technology in human history” and closed the video by saying he thought A.I. would help end cancer and mental illness within a decade.)

For SpaceX’s I.P.O., which at the time was the largest on record, banks erected rocket ships in their lobbies and served space-themed food in their cafeterias to mark the first day of trading. During Friday’s roadshow event at JPMorgan, the bank handed out leather laptop cases and cookies that simply said “Anthropic.”

Some invisible Wall Street forces are working in Anthropic’s favor.

Because of its sizable valuation and new rules allowing large I.P.O.s to enter major stock indexes more quickly, the company will benefit from billions of dollars from passive index funds and exchange-traded funds that will automatically buy its shares in its early weeks of trading. That creates a can’t-miss feeling among investors who actively manage money and want to keep pace with the broader market.

Until now, Anthropic’s growth has also seeped into investors’ stock portfolios in more indirect ways. The A.I. company’s announcements have at times sent software stocks tumbling, for instance.

Dr. Amodei isn’t a brand-new face for many large tech investors. The company raised more than $140 billion privately, including from some of the largest mutual funds, pension funds and sovereign wealth funds, much of it just this year.

Michael Paulus, founder of PCM Encore, a wealth management firm, compared the Anthropic I.P.O. to a promising early-stage start-up investment, on a much a grander scale.

“In the next 10 years, will Anthropic at some point trade down 70 percent, probably?” he said. “Could it be worth 10 times what it’s worth today? It’s also probably true.”

articles.title: Inside Microsoft’s Rush to Get Back Online After a Global Outage
articles.text:
Late into the night Thursday, hundreds of Microsoft engineers and top executives were sitting in their darkened offices or home basements, logged into a video conference triaging a nightmare scenario for a technology company.

The world still runs on email, and much of that is processed through Microsoft Outlook. For hours, a company outage affected hospitals, schools, businesses and Congressional offices in Washington. Even Microsoft’s own staff couldn’t use email.

On the videoconference, Scott Guthrie, the senior most executive overseeing the company’s computing infrastructure, was proposing possible fixes, according to a person familiar with the call who was not authorized to speak publicly. People chewed on fingernails, rubbed their foreheads and debated how to turn off other services to prevent a “stampeding herd” so that as systems come back online, they would not be overwhelmed with new demands and shut back down.

By Friday morning, the company had apologized at least twice. It said it determined that the problem stemmed from a recent upgrade to its network, which shut down some servers, and that the systems were steadily improving. “Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage,” the company said in a statement. “While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration.”

Finally, they had kept the herd at bay.

The prolonged and widespread outage was just the most recent reminder that the technological underpinnings of modern life and business are run through just a handful of major companies. And while cyberattacks and malicious actors can target their systems, sometimes the companies learn the hard way that they can introduce devastating flaws when updating or maintaining their own global systems.

Hospitals, law enforcement and government agencies and other vital services are often left vulnerable — unable to function for hours or days at a time.

Last year, Amazon’s cloud computing services were down for 15 hours and knocked a slew of apps and websites, including Zoom and parts of The New York Times, offline. And in the summer of 2024, a faulty software update by the cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike caused airlines to ground flights, businesses to close early, and surgeries to be rescheduled.

For Microsoft, the problems from this week’s outage are not done yet. The short-term financial fallout should be “manageable,” analysts at the investment bank William Blair wrote in a research note Friday. But they said this prolonged outage is a reputational hit that could make companies and other customers reconsider having so much riding on one technology provider.

“We believe the outage could prompt enterprises to reassess their dependence on Microsoft’s infrastructure,” they wrote.

Outlook and other services affected, including Teams and its A.I. assistant Copilot, are part of Microsoft 365’s cloud subscription business, which is used by more than 450 million people and brought in almost $28 billion in its last quarter, which ended Sept. 30. Online memes joked the offering should be rebranded as Microsoft 364.

These subscriptions are central to the company’s business and the foundation on which it is promoting A.I. tools. Microsoft makes the case to customers that if they keep more data on Microsoft’s systems, they will be able to implement and maximize the benefits of A.I. more easily. Microsoft acknowledged that about 20 different services were impaired by the outage, a reminder that consolidating vendors can also create a bigger single point of failure.

Microsoft first detected the Outlook problems Thursday morning, around 9 a.m. on the West Coast, where the company is headquartered. It soon spread from the Americas around the world.

At first, the company said it thought the cause was an unexpected spike in traffic. Then it determined a large number of the company’s servers in its data centers were down, straining the rest of the system. Even as some servers were brought back online, they would shut down again, like a game of Whac-A-Mole.

Luca Arnaboldi, an assistant professor of cybersecurity at the University of Birmingham in England, said the outage was a reminder that when people use “the cloud,” they are actually relying on servers, which have finite resources.

articles.title: Wales 35-28 New Zealand: Wales beat All Blacks for first time since 1953
articles.text:
Nations Championship

Tries: T Williams, Lake, Griffin, James, Rees-Zammit Cons: Costelow 5

New Zealand (21) 28

Tries: Ratima, Sititi, Fineanganofo, Lakai Cons: Mo'unga 4.

Wales celebrated a first victory against New Zealand in 73 years with a brilliant performance to spark astonishing scenes in Cardiff.

Steve Tandy's unfancied side lifted a nation as they broke a 34-match losing sequence against the All Blacks that stretched back to 1953.

In a nine-try Nations Championship thriller at the Principality Stadium, Wales led 14-0, 21-7 and 35-21 before they held off New Zealand with a wonderful defensive display in the final quarter, led by flankers James Botham and Jac Morgan and lock Dafydd Jenkins.

The home side produced a stunning start with tries from inspirational scrum-half Tomos Williams and captain Dewi Lake inside the first six minutes.

Prop Archie Griffin also added a first-half try, but New Zealand responded with scores from scrum-half Cortez Ratima, number eight Wallace Sititi and wing Fehi Fineanganofo to level the score 21-21 at half-time.

Wales centre Eddie James and wing Louis Rees-Zammit scored early second-half tries before New Zealand flanker Peter Lakai pulled one back.

The remarkable Wales defence followed as they held up the All Blacks three times over the line to stop New Zealand scoring, to evoke wild celebrations.

Wales had won the first three games in this fixture in 1905, 1935 and 1953 but have had to wait more than seven decades for the next.

In 1953 the New Zealand dollar did not exist, Cardiff was not the capital city of Wales and tries were only worth three points.

Sections of the New Zealand media had belittled Welsh rugby before the game, while some bookmakers offered odds of 20-1 for a Wales victory.

Legends such as Sir Gareth Edwards, Alun Wyn Jones, Shane Williams, JPR Williams, Barry John and Phil Bennett had never enjoyed success against New Zealand in a Welsh jersey.

Now Tandy's class of 2026 have written their own chapter in Welsh rugby's history.

The 55,152 was the lowest crowd in the 14 matches between Wales and New Zealand at the Principality Stadium. The fans who stayed away will regret it because it was a day to say "I was there".

Welsh rugby has been in the doldrums for so long, on and off the field, but will hope this famous victory can help galvanise the nation.

This was one of the finest performances in Welsh rugby history and a world apart from the display in the 28-21 win against Japan last weekend.

New Zealand might regret failing to take advantage of France's victory against South Africa on Friday night but they still leapfrog the Springboks to top the southern section with one weekend of regular matches remaining.

Wales made four changes to the side that beat Japan, with Taine Basham making his first Test start in four years by replacing injured number eight Aaron Wainwright.

Leicester wing Gabriel Hamer-Webb was preferred to Josh Adams, who scored two tries against Japan, while lock Adam Beard and flanker Botham came in for Ben Carter and Alex Mann.

New Zealand made eight starting swaps from the team that beat Scotland 43-21, with full-back Beauden Barrett handed the Test captaincy for the first time in his 149th international.

New Zealand's haka was the usual piece of theatre as the All Blacks were lit up by a spotlight and Wales in red.

The hosts reacted quickest from the start with prop Nicky Smith winning a turnover before an excellent long pass from Williams released Rees-Zammit.

The wing chipped ahead and Williams, who New Zealand coach Dave Rennie had highlighted as a pre-match dangerman, pounced for the try.

Wales followed this up with a well-worked forward move and captain Lake latched onto a flat Williams pass to crash over.

It was the first time Wales had led New Zealand by 14 points and the home crowd began to dream.

New Zealand seemed shell-shocked but regathered themselves, and Ratima strolled over for an easy try from an attacking line-out.

Rennie stated before the match they needed to eliminate the threat of Morgan at the breakdown, but they failed to do that when the Wales flanker forced a turnover penalty.

This provided the platform for New Zealand-born Wales full-back Blair Murray to release Rees-Zammit, with only good defensive work by Beauden Barrett preventing a try.

New Zealand's defence kept Wales at bay with some important turnovers before a breathless period of play followed with both sides throwing wild passes.

Once matters had settled down, New Zealand made an unusual decision to go for a scrum in the Wales 22 after being given a penalty. This backfired when the visitors were penalised and it provided the hosts with fresh momentum.

The Wales line-out, which broke down against Japan with six throws going astray, was excellent in the opening quarter and provided the foundation for the third try.

After centre Max Llewellyn was initially denied under the All Blacks' posts, prop Griffin popped up for his second try in two weeks.

New Zealand learned from their earlier error by going for an attacking line-out rather than a scrum and Sititi, who was player of the match in this fixture 12 months ago, eventually dived over.

The All Blacks demonstrated their doggedness at the breakdown by forcing two penalties, while the home line-out began to creak with two overthrows.

New Zealand began to grind away and wing Fineanganofo flopped over with Mo'unga's conversion levelling the scores at half-time.

This was the time we assumed the script would follow the familiar tale of New Zealand pulling away. Wales had other ideas.

The hosts began the second half in the same fashion as the first, with scrum-half Williams again the architect as his long pass allowed James to crash over.

Morgan again tormented New Zealand to force another turnover penalty. Wales decided to go for the try and the decision was justified.

Williams' long pass allowed Rees-Zammit to cross for the fifth try which is the highest amount scored by Wales against New Zealand.

Two tries inside the first six minutes in the first half for Wales. A pair of scores inside eight minutes in the second.

New Zealand again regrouped, with flanker Lakai burrowing over as the All Blacks came within seven points.

Lakai almost inspired a fifth Kiwi try with a fine break but replacement prop Gareth Thomas had other ideas by expertly holding up Sititi over the Wales line, before Botham repeated the feat on hooker Asafo Aumua.

Replacement Wales eight Taine Plumtree gained two important turnovers before Tandy decided to take off his half-backs Williams and Costelow, with Ospreys duo Dan Edwards and Reuben Morgan-Williams tasked to see out the final 16 minutes.

Morgan-Williams and Morgan combined to hold up New Zealand for a third time over the line but the All Blacks onslaught kept coming.

Wales dug deep once more, tapping reserves of strength, discipline and concentration to repel that black wave.

The final whistle delivered the win this side and nation have deserved for so long, reducing players and fans alike to tears of joy.

articles.title: Thomas Tuchel: England boss to remind players of anti-racism protocols before Spain game
articles.text:
Manager Thomas Tuchel will remind England's players of Uefa's anti-racism protocols before Sunday's Nations League fixture against Spain in Madrid.

The match will be England's first in the Spanish capital since a notorious fixture at Real Madrid's Bernabeu stadium in 2004 which was overshadowed by racist chanting aimed at England players.

The Spanish federation was fined last month and ordered to play their next friendly match with a partial stadium closure after fans sang "Islamophobic and xenophobic" chants about Muslims during a game against Egypt.

"We had a same discussion before the Serbia game [in Belgrade in September 2025]," Tuchel said. "There is a protocol in place.

"Maybe we take our five minutes to inform the players about the protocol if there is a precedent [in Madrid]."

European governing body Uefa, the organiser of the Nations League, has a three-step protocol to handle incidents of discrimination inside stadiums, designed to give referees the power to halt matches, and even abandon games if racist behaviour continues.

In the first instance, referees halt the match and request an announcement on the public address system.

Then, if discrimination continues, officials can stop the game for five to 10 minutes and take the players from the field.

If issues continue after the second stoppage, then the game can be abandoned.

"It's important that the players know about the protocol," Tuchel said.

"And then, yeah, we will give our answers if stuff like this happens. Best answers are on the pitch."

articles.title: Jesus Owono: Tenerife boss Alvaro Cervera says 12-game ban 'might seem light' but accepts rules
articles.text:
Tenerife manager Alvaro Cervera says that goalkeeper Jesus Owono's 12-match ban "might feel light" but he accepts that the regulations do not "specifically account for what happened".

FC Andorra's Owono, 25, was sent off after colliding with Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel during the closing stages of the Spanish second-tier match between their two respective sides on 2 November.

De Miguel died the following day aged 30, and a disciplinary committee from the Spanish football federation confirmed Owono's suspension on Friday.

It was the maximum punishment that he could have received as the disciplinary committee could only consider the offence on the pitch and not "the tragic outcome of the incident".

"I think that, just as in other areas of life, there are rules or laws that must be followed," said Cervera, speaking before his club's fixture against Ceuta on Sunday - their first match since De Miguel's death.

"Since the current regulations don't specifically account for what happened, I believe they have simply adhered to the rules and imposed the number of matches permitted by the regulations.

"Anything else I might say would just be my own personal opinion, which I'll keep to myself. It might seem a bit light when compared to other cases, but in reality, I don't think the rules allow for anything else."

The disciplinary committee also said it had to base its decision "on the facts expressly recorded in the referee's report", which stated the player "was sent off for 'violently striking an opponent in the chest with his leg, using excessive force, while the ball was in play'".

Cervera, 61, also described the experience of returning to training and preparing for their next match as "tough" and "complicated".

"When we're together, we're fine, during our sessions, we're doing well," he said.

"It feels like the group is gradually getting back to normal. What we don't know is how everyone is doing when we're apart and that's a significant factor.

"Everyone has their own way of coping and their own thoughts; some have people at home to support them, while others are more on their own.

"We're making progress, a very slow process, but we are moving forward - it's tough, it's complicated."

He also said that he was not sure whether his players were ready to return to playing, describing how some would appreciate a distraction and others will not be in the right frame of mind yet.

"Both positions are reasonable," Cervera added.

"On one hand, you want to return to some sense of normality though you know that true normality isn't something you'll find right now.

"This isn't something you can just set aside or push to the back of your mind to focus on your own work; it's not like other life events you might encounter. It's always there, constantly on your mind, yet we have to keep going."

articles.title: Sandpaper scandal: David Warner accuses Cricket Australia of 'cover-up'
articles.text:
David Warner has accused Cricket Australia (CA) of a "cover up" as the row over the 2018 ball-tampering scandal continued.

Former vice-captain Warner, captain Steve Smith and opener Cameron Bancroft all served lengthy bans as part of CA's investigation into the ball-tampering scandal that rocked Australian cricket during a Test series in South Africa in 2018.

Batter Usman Khawaja has reopened discussions about the scandal with explosive claims in his new autobiography, where he said the entire Australia team knew about the use of sandpaper to tamper with the ball.

And Warner has questioned the investigation into the incident by claiming that Australia's bowlers from the Cape Town Test were not interviewed.

"As far as l am aware, CA did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation," Warner said.

"If that's correct, then how can CA push the idea that the bowlers didn't know?

"It looks like they had decided who they wanted to blame from the very beginning, ran a shoddy investigation to serve the purpose and now they want to maintain the false narrative that the bowlers had no idea.

"That stinks of a cover-up."

The four frontline bowlers - Hazlewood, Starc, Lyon and Pat Cummins - have maintained they did not know about the plan to use sandpaper to tamper with the ball.

Cummins, Australia's Test captain since 2021, said in his extraordinary news conference on Friday that he was interviewed as part of the investigation.

In response to Warner's comments, CA said: "As we have stated previously, all players were given the opportunity to speak at the time of the initial investigation and have had the ability to come forward with new evidence in the eight years since.

"Subsequently, CA has respected every player and former players' right to provide their own version of events."

articles.title: DP World Tour Championship: Tyrrell Hatton leads as Rory McIlroy fades
articles.text:
DP World Tour Championship third-round leaderboard

-9 T Hatton (Eng); -8 V Perez (Fra); -6 M Lindberg (Swe); -5 A Scott (Aus), E Chacarra (Spa), F Laporta (Ita), R McIlroy (NI)

Selected others: -4 D Bradbury (Eng), J Schaper (SA), K Reitan (Nor); -3 M Wallace (Eng), J Dean (Eng), J Rahm (Spa); +3 P Reed (US), T Fleetwood (Eng)

Rory McIlroy's hopes of winning a record-equalling eighth Race to Dubai title faded as he fell four shots behind leader Tyrrell Hatton after three rounds of the season-ending DP World Tour Championship.

Northern Irishman McIlroy started Saturday tied for the lead with Hatton but, while the Englishman remained at the top of the field with a four-under-par 68, McIlroy fell away with a 72 at the Earth Course in Dubai.

Hatton, on nine under for the tournament, holds a one-shot lead over France's Victor Perez as he bids for a first DP World Tour Championship, while Sweden's Mikael Lindberg is third on six under.

McIlroy is joint fourth in a group of four players which includes Spain's Eugenio Chacarra, the current leader in the Race to Dubai standings.

Six-time major champion McIlroy began the tournament trailing Chacarra by more than 500 points, but knowing a win would guarantee him an eighth season-long crown to equal the tally set by Scotland's Colin Montgomerie.

McIlroy also has a chance of winning the title if he finishes in the top four and Chacarra falls down the order.

He took the outright lead with an eagle three on the par-five seventh, before bogeys on the eighth, ninth and 10th.

A birdie on the 14th was followed by another dropped shot on the 15th, but McIlroy finished with a birdie at the par-five 18th after narrowly missing a six-foot eagle putt.

Hatton scrambled a par at the last after driving into the water and finding a greenside bunker with his approach shot.

He will play alongside Perez, who carded a 67, on the final day.

"It would mean a lot to go on and win tomorrow," said Hatton.

"There is a lot that can change. The course is playing difficult this week and there's a lot of fantastic players just behind. It is going to be a tough day."

Spain's Jon Rahm, who could clinch the Race to Dubai title with victory on Sunday, fell six shots off the lead with a third consecutive 71.

Chacarra, four shots adrift off the lead after two rounds, carded a 68 that included nine birdies, three bogeys and a double bogey.

McIlroy will play alongside Englishman Dan Bradbury, who climbed to four under with a stunning 66.

Lindberg will play in the penultimate group alongside Australia's 2013 Masters winner Adam Scott, who went round a 67.

articles.title: Will John McGinn take Kenny Dalglish and Denis Law's joint record for most Scotland goals?
articles.text:
As Scotland legend Kenny Dalglish watched one of his records equalled in Scotland's 2-1 win over North Macedonia, another of his feats loomed into view.

The night was supposed to be about Andy Robertson joining Dalglish as Scotland's most-capped man, the Tottenham left-back making his 102nd appearance for his country.

But instead, for the first time, the 75-year-old might be nervous that his crown as one of Scotland men's all-time top goalscorers is wobbling.

That is because, in Scotland's rather humdrum Nations League victory, John McGinn - in his 94th Scotland appearance - took two big strides towards the record.

The Aston Villa midfielder now has 24 goals for his country - six shy of Dalglish's long-standing record of 30, shared with Denis Law.

"It's something that's been in the back of my head," McGinn admitted in the post-match debrief. "If I start climbing that table, it means we've been successful as a team."

Now 32 years old, time is running out for him. But as he pulls level with Hughie Gallacher, one of the Wembley Wizards of folklore, his ambition is clear.

There was a time when talk of this record being toppled seemed laughable. Scotland has produced strikers in recent decades, but none close to Dalglish or Law.

The fact a midfielder might take the title makes McGinn's feat all the more astonishing.

His prowess in front of goal is no secret to the Tartan Army. There was the spell at the end of 2019 where he scored six in three games, his overhead kick against Austria, his late winner against Croatia in 2024.

But of late, his lack of goals and even his performances have had some fans questioning where he fits into the Scotland team.

"It has been a bit of a dry patch for me over the last year on the goal front," McGinn admitted, and he's not wrong.

He failed to find the back of the net for Scotland in 2025, the first time he'd done that since 2020.

But, just as his form at Villa has sky-rocketed, he came up big for his new international head coach Sebastien Pocognoli.

"Isn't it great to have a John McGinn in your team?" former Scotland winger Pat Nevin said on Sportsound. "He's somebody you'd want to have in your team to be taking a penalty for you.

"I'd be surprised if John McGinn doesn't get the goal record now. It might take him another year or two, but he is definitely capable of getting that record."

Becoming Scotland's main penalty taker will help, a fact McGinn alluded to coyly post-match.

In his career, he had only taken one spot-kick before this season - scoring for Scotland in the 3-3 draw against Norway back in 2023.

In this campaign he has scored three and missed one, smacking the bar against Fulham on Halloween.

In classic McGinn fashion, he bounced back to slot home against Manchester United the following week, before being caught on ref-cam admitting to the official that he was nervous to take it after his hitting the woodwork.

That jovial, lovable personality has not just won him fans off the pitch. It is clear that his team-mates at both Villa and the national team adore him.

"He's not going to stop until he [gets the record]," said striker Che Adams, who helped set up McGinn's first against North Macedonia.

"Everyone's pleased for him, he's the best person I've met in football. For him to get the recognition he deserves is amazing."

McGinn's iconic status in Scottish football is secure and will not be tarnished if he fails to climb the mountain.

Whether it is being speared by Steven Thompson in training, calling Scotland performances 'jobby', or admitting he would "probably be at Yeovil" were it not for his backside, the midfielder has already won the heart of a nation.

articles.title: Vaibhav Sooryavanshi: India teenager becomes youngest captain in men's T20 cricket
articles.text:
Teenage sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi has become the youngest captain in top-level men's Twenty20 cricket after taking charge of his state side Bihar on Saturday.

Captaining at the age of 15 years and 232 days, Sooryavanshi broke the record held by Zach Vukusic, who captained Croatia aged 17 years and 311 days.

Bihar lost their opening match in the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy - India's domestic state T20 competition, below the Indian Premier League (IPL) - by five wickets to Saurashtra, with Sooryavanshi making 18 from 12 balls.

It is the latest landmark the young career of Sooryavanshi, who became India's youngest men's international in July when he made his T20 debut against England.

He has broken numerous records since making his IPL debut for Rajasthan Royals as a 14-year-old in 2025, becoming the franchise tournament's youngest player.

He became the youngest centurion in men's T20s when hitting a hundred against Gujarat Titans later that season, and this year was the tournament's leading run-scorer.

Sooryavanshi played in two of India's five T20 internationals in New Zealand earlier this month, with a top score of 45 in the third match in Wellington.

He is also due to be part of India's side at the Rising Stars Asia Cup, a development 50-over tournament which takes place in Doha later this month.

articles.title: Mauricio Pochettino: What can Manchester United fans expect from new boss?
articles.text:
Mauricio Pochettino heads to Old Trafford with a reputation for "brutal" pre-seasons, an obsession with fitness and a no-nonsense approach.

Manchester United confirmed on Friday that Pochettino will become their manager on 18 November - replacing Michael Carrick - and has signed a contract until June 2029.

So what should the players and staff expect when the Argentine takes control at the end of next week?

BBC Sport spoke to Toby Alderweireld, who spent four years playing for Pochettino at Tottenham during a successful period where they reached the Champions League final and finished second in the Premier League.

Alderweireld, 37, says Pochettino has a no-nonsense approach to management and that he can get the best out of a squad, as long as you do it his way.

"He is very approachable but you need to follow his plan. If you don't follow his plan, you go on the side and you're not coming back any more.

"You need to think about team, team, team. If you're thinking about yourself, you're gone.

"As a player you have your own life, your own situation but he says 'look, I understand and you can talk to me about it but the team is number one' - that's the way it is and if you're not following it, he'll put you on the sideline.

"He's straightforward, has his own ideas and maybe you agree with them or don't, that's up to you. But you need to follow him and I think that's something Manchester United need - a big character, everyone in the same direction, following the plan and if not, no problem, you can go. He's the main man.

"He's a very smart man, knows how to talk to the press and what to say. He will create an environment like 'it's us against the world' - we are getting fit, we are together as a team. It doesn't matter what people say, let's work together and get results together.

"At Spurs there was coaching staff but he will be there. He knows everything. If he's not there, he's looking at video and data. He knows everything about the players on and off the pitch - the players will be watched.

"He is, in a positive way, a control freak because he says your body is your weapon and it needs to be ready to perform."

Manchester United have been criticised this season for an apparent lack of fitness and for not running enough in games - they rank in the bottom five in the league for distance covered and most high-intensity runs.

Alderweireld says Pochettino's number one demand is fitness and running.

"First of all he made us very fit. Pre-season was brutal.

"The way he wants to play - on the front foot, putting people under pressure, a high line, very dynamic play - you need to run. You need to be capable of running and be capable of high intensity runs - the basic is to be fit.

"Every manager wants a good pre-season and time to give the players their ideas and the fitness. But the players are going to feel straight away that it's a different level.

"This is every day at the training ground, it's 100% - that's what he asks, what he demands. It will be a big difference for the players and they're going to see results there straight away.

"In the Champions League semi-final, we were 3-0 down [against Ajax] and he didn't have a tactical half-time talk. He just said 'you're going to be physical, you're going to fight, you only need one goal to be back in the game, believe that everything is possible'.

"That was a big moment because we were nowhere near Ajax at that time, especially in that game. But we changed everything by intensity, by duels. I remember the long ball to [Fernando] Llorente and just fighting and asking 'how badly do you want it?' It changed from that moment."

Manchester United confirmed on Friday that Pochettino will become their manager on 18 November - replacing Michael Carrick - and has signed a contract until June 2029. So what...

articles.title: Sources: Vikings made initial Kirk Cousins trade call to Raiders before MNF
articles.text:
The first time the Vikings reached out to the Raiders about a potential trade for Kirk Cousins was midday Monday, hours before Minnesota played the Bills on "Monday Night Football," league sources told ESPN and NFL Network.

During that call, the Vikings made it clear to the Raiders that they wanted to see how Monday night went first before having any further conversations about Cousins, but they would be in touch if needed.

Bright and early the next morning, hours after Minnesota's offensive meltdown, the Vikings called the Raiders before 6 a.m. PT and set the wheels in motion for a potential Cousins trade.

It was not a deal the Raiders wanted or were looking to make, especially when Minnesota's initial offer was a fifth-round draft pick, according to sources.

But once the Vikings upped their offer to a third-round pick, the Raiders had discussions about whether the trade made sense, and here's where they landed:

Not only would they be receiving a third-round pick, but they also would free up $10 million in cash for the 2027 season, as the bonus guarantee owed to Cousins would shift to Minnesota's responsibility. It was not a trade that the Raiders enjoyed making, but one they believed would be in the best interests of the organization.

The Raiders also believed 2026 No. 1 pick Fernando Mendoza has looked, in the word of one source, "phenomenal" in practice. There never was going to be a right time to insert Mendoza into the starting lineup, but Minnesota made this as good a time as any.

Cousins will start Sunday against the Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field, and Mendoza will make his first career start against the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks.

Competition committee to discuss trade snafus

The NFL's competition committee is expected to discuss a potential solution after multiple trades this week were voided or altered, according to sources.

In the last week alone, the Bengals declined to make a trade for linebacker Arnold Ebiketie after agreeing to terms with the Eagles; the Lions and Jets altered the compensation they initially agreed to in a trade for safety Andre Cisco; and the Broncos voided a trade with the Chargers for Daiyan Henley after concerns about the linebacker's knee and the sides were unable to agree to revised compensation.

Last offseason, the Raiders and Ravens agreed to a Maxx Crosby trade before the star pass rusher failed his physical and the deal was voided.

Now front office executives are complaining, and the competition committee is expected to address the issue during the offseason.

Various front office executives last week pointed out that trade terms should not be negotiable once they are agreed to, as the Lions attempted to do in a deal for Cisco and the Broncos attempted to do with Henley.

Chargers coach Jim Harbaugh said as much to reporters Thursday, asserting that the loophole in the NFL's trade system needs to be closed so that teams cannot back out of deals.

The Eagles were not pleased that the Bengals reneged on their deal for Ebiketie after learning they would lose a third-round compensatory pick, and the Chargers were unhappy that the Broncos tried to change the terms on their deal for Henley after he took a physical that led to questions about his knee.

It is an issue that bears watching this offseason, and some around the league believe rule modifications are in order.

A possible solution would be preventing the teams from altering draft picks after a trade is agreed upon, only giving teams the option to accept or not.

The Jaguars and Bills will be in competition to represent the AFC in the Super Bowl, but both were in competition for some of the same players ahead of Tuesday's trade deadline.

The two teams that were most aggressive in trading for Eagles defensive tackle Jordan Davis were the Bills and Jaguars, who wound up trading a first- and second-round pick to the Eagles.

The two teams most aggressive for former Falcons safety Jessie Bates also were the Bills and Jaguars, who traded second- and fifth-round picks to Atlanta.

After the Jaguars traded for Davis and Bates, the Bills pivoted to two safeties: Arizona's Budda Baker and Tennessee's Amani Hooker. The Cardinals declined to trade their respected veteran safety, but the Titans listened and agreed to trade Hooker and a fifth-round pick to the Bills for a second-round pick.

In the end, two of the AFC's best each got better. They competed for some of the same players and now are expected to be competing for the AFC championship.

Keeping up with the Joneses

The San Francisco 49ers left no doubt how much they value quarterback Mac Jones.

When the Vikings called San Francisco as part of due diligence in their search for a quarterback, sources told ESPN that Niners general manager John Lynch informed Minnesota brass that it would take a second-round pick and more for Jones. Perhaps a second-rounder and a middle-round pick might have gotten a trade done.

Instead, because of the high cost associated with the veteran quarterback, the conversations ended there and Jones remains a valued member of the 49ers.

This was not the first time the teams had spoken about Jones in a possible trade and not the first time San Francisco had set a price that high. Niners coach Kyle Shanahan views Jones as a franchise-caliber quarterback and would trade him only for a deal they had no choice but to accept.

To add to that value, Jones won four of his first five starts in place of the injured Brock Purdy last year despite battling injuries of his own and ended up with a 5-3 record and a QB rating of 97.4 for the season.

In the final year of his two-year, $8.41 million contract, Jones is a free agent after the season.

The Packers and Broncos checked in on Titans running back Tony Pollard, whom Tennessee would not have traded for anything less than a third-round pick.

While the Eagles traded stars in Davis and center Cam Jurgens in the flurry leading up to the deadline, they held off trading another player who was wanted -- Dallas Goedert.

Sources said several teams inquired about the pass-catching tight end, including the 49ers. But Goedert, 31, never got close to being traded. He remains in Philadelphia and could even re-sign with the Eagles for 2027.
